touches.text: A question is [Q#n: ...]. Its #n is its own and never changes; a new question takes the next unused number, which is 88. An answered question disappears: what stays is the answer and its why, written into the outline.

The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien. Akien, 2026-11-11, Q#85: "you and me. later there will be a specific agent for it, but that's so far off we're not even thinking about it now except 'after the outline is implemented'." So until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both of us read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, "leaving the more capable in case a bigger one comes along."

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf (Akien, same day: "that could be in the class, rather than the instance :) self queuing"). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "now it has to send it's fileref over to the thing that will process it, and a new code instance created over there even tho it's the same thing... because that's good encapsulation. :)"
Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
Has its own workflow stamped on it (the state string, with the cursor). Each workflow step declares what it needs.

Ideas and questions are not tickets. An idea is a note that leads to an intention, and stops mattering once the intention is set down. A question exists only to deduce the why: once answered, what matters is the answer and the why, and nothing else.
Knowledge: one list of nodes, owned by the librarian.

Ownership. The librarian owns every tree and delegates some to the devices that learn. EVERYTHING THAT LEARNS USING OUR GRAPH TREES IS A DELEGATE (CodeMother, chart and any learning block are examples, not a list), and each holds its trees by the librarian's delegation (Law 6: delegation through the owner's gate). WHY: two holders with different weights over the same nodes have different perspectives and can debate points, and the librarian, asked anything, can look at the query from both.
Shareable provenance (charters, tickets, validations) is git JSON beside the code, never a row.
Answering a question is the operator acting, so it is `cairn operator answer <id> "<words>"`, never a verb on whichever device asked.

VERBS: activate, charter, deposit, drain, feedback, question, sealed (plus get and show). Moving a ticket across its workflow is the ticket's own act; CodeMother's gates only answer it (3.3.4). Each chart stage (orient through validate) and the verdict is a gate machine that answers queueme <fileref>; the ticket class queues itself to each in turn (3.3.4.3), so there is no chart or verdict verb, and `cross` leaves with the harbor's `clear` (9.4.1.5). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10, Q#81 ("should CodeMother answer a `chart` verb ... and a `verdict` verb?"): "yes, Q#81 closes on that", that being each stage and the verdict a gate with queueme, queued by the ticket class.

artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record.

chain: the grammar every chart stage speaks. WHY: one grammar lets stages chain in any order. USERS: CodeMother (heaviest), base, tester, rehearsal, build_inspector, proof_coverage, aider, skills/chart.
charter: compiles a component's bounded state from its history. WHY: state is compiled from the component's tickets, never hand-edited (Law 5). Held by CodeMother.

question: the open-question door: a decision only the operator can make, bound to its ticket, answered in the operator's words. WHY: a spec choice is settled by Akien's head, recorded verbatim, never by a paragraph of CC's. USERS: tickets and CodeMother open them; the operator answers (7.4.2).
ticket_inspector: completeness checks over tickets at rest. [why?] USERS: CodeMother.
